reference.source: Green's Operative Hand Surgery / Campbell's Operative Orthopaedics
clinicalPearls: Presents with pain and swelling on the dorsoradial forearm a short distance proximal to the wrist, above the extensor retinaculum
The site corresponds to where the first dorsal compartment tendons cross over the second compartment
The first compartment (abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis) crosses the second (extensor carpi radialis longus and brevis) at an oblique angle
Friction at the crossover produces a tenosynovitis or peritendinous inflammation of the second compartment
There may be palpable crepitus or a squeak, sometimes likened to wet leather, over the affected area
It is an overuse condition seen in rowers, weightlifters, racquet sports and skiers
It is distinguished from de Quervain tenosynovitis, which occurs more distally at the radial styloid within the first compartment
Generic management includes activity modification, wrist splinting and corticosteroid injection into the second compartment, with surgical release rarely required
reference.pathophysiology: Intersection syndrome arises from repetitive wrist flexion and extension causing friction where the first dorsal compartment tendons, the abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis, cross obliquely over the second compartment tendons, the extensor carpi radialis longus and brevis, a few centimetres proximal to Lister tubercle. The friction sets up a tenosynovitis and peritendinous inflammation with oedema, and sometimes an adventitial bursitis, producing the pain, swelling and crepitus that characterise the condition.
additionalDifferentials: De Quervain tenosynovitis at the radial styloid
Wartenberg syndrome from superficial radial nerve irritation
Distal radius stress injury or fracture
Wrist osteoarthritis, for example scaphotrapeziotrapezoid or radioscaphoid
additionalInvestigations: Clinical localisation of tenderness proximal to the wrist with crepitus over the crossover
Ultrasound demonstrating peritendinous fluid and oedema at the intersection
MRI when the diagnosis is uncertain or to exclude other pathology
Plain radiographs to exclude a bony cause such as fracture or arthritis
The Finkelstein test to help differentiate the condition from de Quervain tenosynovitis
redFlags: Signs of infection suggesting a septic tenosynovitis
An underlying fracture or bony injury
Features of compartment compromise after acute trauma
Neurological signs indicating superficial radial nerve involvement
reference.prognosis: The condition is generally self-limiting and resolves with rest and conservative treatment, though it may recur if the provoking activity is not modified.
pitfalls: Confusing it with de Quervain tenosynovitis, which lies at a different site and is treated differently
Failing to modify the provoking activity, leading to recurrence
management: Modify activity with relative rest and avoidance of the provoking repetitive wrist flexion and extension
Apply thumb-spica or wrist splinting to rest the first and second dorsal compartment tendons
Use ice and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs for pain and peritendinous inflammation
Consider corticosteroid injection into the second-compartment tendon sheath for refractory symptoms
Refer for physiotherapy with graded stretching, strengthening and correction of technique and ergonomics before return to sport
Reserve surgical decompression and tenosynovectomy of the second dorsal compartment for cases failing conservative measures

flowcharts.title: Diagnosis and management of Intersection syndrome

nodes.text: Dorsoradial forearm pain and swelling a short distance above the wrist
Signs of infection, fracture or compartment compromise after trauma?
Exclude septic tenosynovitis or fracture; urgent orthopaedic review
Clinical localisation, ultrasound, radiographs, Finkelstein test, MRI if uncertain
Pain at second-compartment crossover with no bony or styloid cause?
Consider de Quervain tenosynovitis, Wartenberg syndrome or fracture
Relative rest and avoidance of repetitive wrist movements
Corticosteroid injection into second-compartment sheath if refractory
Settles with rest and splinting; surgery reserved for failure
